PullRequest.Title: Add built-in Markdown task progress and live widget themes
PullRequest.Body:
## Summary
- Add a built-in `widget:task-progress` fenced-code-block contribution, bundled into a self-contained HTML guest.
- Count completed and total tasks from the document AST and update on checkbox/source edits.
- Add localized accessible progress, animation, reduced-motion support, and transparent guest styling.
- Forward VS Code theme tokens and explicit light/dark color-scheme changes to live embedded editors.
- Add focused unit and browser regressions for progress, theme changes, frame reuse, border geometry and padding.

## Dependency / merge order
https://github.com/microsoft/vscode-packages/pull/349 is merged and published as `@vscode/markdown-editor@0.0.2-121`. The dependency and lockfile now use that release. Its npm `gitHead` matches merged commit `8d863f11c9833d3e752c87b796435d7d597f41f5`. No machine-local `file:` override is included.

## Validation
Before extraction, in the existing development checkout with the companion local package: renderer build/typecheck/ESLint, extension-host typecheck/build, and 7 task-progress tests including browser regressions passed. No dependency installation or tests were run in this main-based PR worktree, as requested.

Only task-owned hunks were moved. Outline, active-block highlighting, source-edit work, image-paste changes and local-development dependency overrides remain outside this PR.

### Published dependency validation
- Verified the published tarball against the lockfile integrity hash.
- Generated manifest consistency check passed against the published commands.
- Renderer and self-contained guest bundled successfully in memory against the published package.
- Full renderer TypeScript check passed against the published declarations, including the theme-change API.
- No dependencies installed or tests run in the PR worktree; validation reused existing development dependencies.

Findings.ConfidenceRationale: The default empty provider state, exact providers.length lazy-load condition, unconditional added provider, and dynamic import call path are all directly traced. Only the absolute duration varies by machine and cache warmth.
Findings.PerformanceResource: Dynamic module bytes plus JavaScript parsing/evaluation and iframe-factory initialization
Findings.PerformanceScaling: Once per live Markdown editor webview that contains at least one fenced code block, even when none use widget:task-progress; opening multiple editor webviews repeats initialization in each isolated webview context.
Findings.PerformanceOutcome: Increased live-editor open/render latency and CPU work for ordinary Markdown documents with fenced code
Findings.PreviousBehavior: The external provider list defaults to empty, and LazyCodeBlockEditorFactory.create only starts its dynamic import when providers.length is nonzero, so documents with ordinary fences and no contributed providers did not load @vscode/markdown-editor/web-editors.
Findings.ChangedBehavior: Appending the built-in task-progress provider makes the list permanently non-empty. The first ordinary fenced block now causes LazyCodeBlockEditorFactory to import and construct VirtualizedIframeEmbeddedEditorFactory before provider selection can reject the block's language.
Findings.CausalDiffEvidence: The added `this.#taskProgressProvider` at editor.ts:611 changes `#createIframeProviders([])` from an empty array to a non-empty array. The unchanged lazy factory gates `#loadFactory()` solely on `this.#providers.length`, while the existing provider field defaults to `[]`.
Findings.Title: Keep ordinary code blocks from loading the iframe editor subsystem
Findings.Impact: Opening a live Markdown editor on a normal document containing an ordinary fenced snippet now loads and evaluates the iframe-editor implementation and constructs its factory. This delays rendering once per editor webview; warm resource caches may avoid transfer but not per-webview module evaluation/initialization.
Findings.Evidence: editor.ts initializes `#codeBlockEditorProviders` to `[]`, passes the result of `#createIframeProviders` to LazyCodeBlockEditorFactory, and the changed line always appends the built-in provider. lazyCodeBlockEditorFactory.ts:create states that creation is invoked for a block and starts `#loadFactory()` whenever providers.length is nonzero; its loader dynamically imports `@vscode/markdown-editor/web-editors`. Therefore any first fenced block, not only `widget:task-progress`, crosses the module-load boundary after this change.
Findings.Recommendation: Preserve the lazy guard by triggering the iframe-editor import only when the current block matches an available provider (in particular, gate the built-in provider on the exact `widget:task-progress` language), while retaining existing external-provider selection semantics.

Findings.ConfidenceRationale: The static import chain and nested bundling are explicit in the changed build and provider code. Bundle size is not measured, so magnitude is uncertain, but inclusion and per-webview allocation are deterministic.
Findings.PerformanceResource: Bundled HTML/JavaScript bytes and the resulting startup string allocation
Findings.PerformanceScaling: A fixed duplicate guest payload is loaded and allocated once for every live Markdown editor webview, including documents with no code blocks; concurrent editor tabs multiply the retained strings, while cold opens also pay resource transfer.
Findings.PerformanceOutcome: Larger editor startup payload, additional parse/allocation work, and increased retained memory
Findings.PreviousBehavior: The sole editor entry did not contain a task-progress guest application, so opening a live Markdown editor loaded no task-progress HTML or guest-side WebEditorClient code.
Findings.ChangedBehavior: The provider statically imports taskProgress.html. The build plugin first bundles taskProgressGuest.ts and its @vscode/web-editors dependency into a self-contained HTML string, then emits that string as a JavaScript module; because editor.ts statically imports the provider, this opaque guest payload is included on every editor startup even though resolve may never be called.
Findings.CausalDiffEvidence: The new static import `import taskProgressHtml from './taskProgress.html'` at line 11 is reachable through editor.ts's static provider import. esbuild.markdownEditor.mts has one `editor.ts` entry and converts this HTML import to `export default <JSON string>` after separately bundling the guest.
Findings.Title: Load the self-contained task-progress guest only when resolved
Findings.Impact: Even a plain Markdown document with no `widget:task-progress` fence downloads/reads, parses as a literal, allocates, and retains the entire self-contained iframe app in its webview. The cost repeats across editor webviews and is absent before this PR.
Findings.Evidence: buildTaskProgressHtml.mts bundles taskProgressGuest.ts with esbuild and injects it inline into the template. taskProgressGuest.ts imports WebEditorClient from @vscode/web-editors. The outer build has a single editor.ts entry; taskProgressProvider is statically imported and its static HTML import is returned by the plugin as an ordinary JS module, so splitting cannot defer this opaque string. markdownEditorProvider.ts loads editor.js for every live editor.
Findings.Recommendation: Make the HTML module a dynamic import inside `resolve` (or emit it as a separate asset) so esbuild creates a guest chunk fetched only after an exact task-progress fence is selected.

Findings.ConfidenceRationale: The observable dependency, synchronous autorun, exhaustive traversal, and edit reachability are directly visible and tested. The exact milliseconds depend on document size, so severity reflects magnitude uncertainty rather than mechanism uncertainty.
Findings.PerformanceResource: Synchronous CPU traversal of every Markdown AST node
Findings.PerformanceScaling: O(number of AST nodes) for every document observable invalidation while at least one task-progress transport is active. The shared derived value correctly keeps this to one traversal per edit rather than one per widget, but repeated keystrokes still produce repeated whole-document walks.
Findings.PerformanceOutcome: Additional input latency and main-thread CPU usage in large Markdown documents
Findings.PreviousBehavior: Edits updated the editor model without a task-progress-specific whole-AST traversal.
Findings.ChangedBehavior: The new derived observable calls countTasks whenever model.document changes. Each active transport autoruns that derived value, and countTasks performs an explicit stack walk over every node before checking whether the task totals actually changed.
Findings.CausalDiffEvidence: The added expression `derived(reader => countTasks(model.document.read(reader)))` at line 19 directly places countTasks behind every document invalidation; added lines 47-57 show countTasks pushes every child and exhausts the full tree.
Findings.Title: Move full-document task recounts off the per-edit path
Findings.Impact: With a task-progress widget open in a large Markdown file, every keystroke or source update adds a collection-wide AST pass on the UI thread, increasing typing/paste latency even when no task changed.
Findings.Evidence: TaskProgressHostTransport constructs an autorun synchronously over the shared derived observable. The browser/unit tests demonstrate source replacement and checkbox edits immediately publish updated values. `countTasks` always walks all descendants, and only after it completes does the transport compare checked/total and suppress an unchanged message. Thus typing unrelated text in a document containing the widget still pays the full traversal.
Findings.Recommendation: Coalesce document invalidations and compute from only the latest AST off the immediate edit turn, or maintain task totals incrementally from changed subtrees; continue sharing one result across all widget transports and publish the latest count.

Scenarios.Scenario: Open a live Markdown editor for a plain document with no task-progress fence
Scenarios.CriticalPath: The webview must load and evaluate editor.js before the live editor is usable. The new self-contained task-progress HTML is statically reachable from that entry and therefore sits on this critical path even though its provider resolve function is never called.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Load the packaged editor.js webview resource, now containing the opaque self-contained task-progress guest string
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: One editor.js resource load per editor webview, with cache reuse possible for bytes; the added payload is present for every load regardless of document content.
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: editor.js was already loaded, but it did not include the separately bundled task-progress guest/WebEditorClient application.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: The resource must load before editor startup completes; the added guest bytes increase this existing critical-path operation.

Scenarios.ScalingInput: One fixed guest payload per editor webview; memory and parse/allocation work multiply with concurrently open live Markdown editors.
Scenarios.EffectiveConcurrency: Each editor has an isolated webview context and performs its own evaluation/allocation. Browser resource caching may coalesce or cache byte reads across editors, but it does not share the resulting JavaScript heap string between webviews.
Scenarios.CacheBehavior: On a cold load, the enlarged editor.js must be read/transferred in full. On a warm resource cache, transfer can be avoided, but each webview still parses the module and allocates/retains the embedded HTML string. No negative-cache behavior applies.
Scenarios.MechanismConfidence: High: the single entry, static import chain, nested guest bundle, and unconditional editor.js load are explicit.
Scenarios.MagnitudeUncertainty: The generated guest's exact compressed and in-memory sizes were not available from repository sources, so absolute startup milliseconds and bytes are uncertain.
Scenarios.Verdict: Reportable eager-startup regression because task-progress-only bytes are deterministically loaded and retained for documents that never request the feature.

Scenarios.Scenario: Open a live Markdown document containing an ordinary fenced code block but no task-progress fence or external embedded-editor provider
Scenarios.CriticalPath: Rendering encounters the fenced block and calls LazyCodeBlockEditorFactory.create. Because the changed provider list is now non-empty, create starts the dynamic web-editors import and later refreshes the view; this work is unnecessary for the ordinary block.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Dynamically load the @vscode/markdown-editor/web-editors chunk from the packaged webview resources
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: One newly reachable dynamic resource load per editor webview with at least one ordinary fence; coalesced across all fences in that editor.
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: With the default empty external-provider list, providers.length was zero and ordinary fences did not start this dynamic import.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: Starts during fenced-block rendering and factory completion triggers a view refresh, adding startup/render CPU and latency.

Scenarios.ScalingInput: Triggered once by the first fenced block per editor webview, not once per block, because #loadStarted coalesces subsequent create calls.
Scenarios.EffectiveConcurrency: The lazy factory permits one in-flight module load per editor via #loadStarted. Multiple editor webviews can independently load/initialize the subsystem concurrently.
Scenarios.CacheBehavior: Cold cache pays resource I/O/transfer plus parse/evaluation. A warm resource cache may avoid byte transfer, but each isolated webview still evaluates the module and constructs a factory. Failed loads are not retried in that factory instance because #loadStarted remains true.
Scenarios.MechanismConfidence: Very high: the list changes from empty to permanently non-empty, and the lazy guard checks only list length before importing.
Scenarios.MagnitudeUncertainty: Exact chunk size and device-specific load/evaluation duration are uncertain; ordinary fenced code is a common enough input that the trigger is realistic.
Scenarios.Verdict: Reportable eager-work regression; the feature-specific subsystem now loads for unrelated code fences.

Scenarios.Scenario: Render one or more widget:task-progress fences and edit the Markdown source
Scenarios.CriticalPath: Initial widget rendering resolves the provider, creates an iframe/transport per live widget, and computes the document-wide task totals before publishing. On each document invalidation, the shared derived count synchronously traverses the current AST; changed totals are then sent to each ready widget.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Cross-frame host-transport readiness and task-progress update messages
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: One ready exchange per created widget transport and one update per ready widget when checked/total changes; unchanged totals suppress update fan-out.
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: No task-progress frames or associated cross-frame messages existed.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: Initial ready/update messaging is required before each widget displays current progress; subsequent messages are on the live-update path.

Scenarios.ScalingInput: The recount is O(total AST nodes) once per document update after sharing/caching, while publication and iframe messaging scale with the number of ready task-progress widgets. Visible widgets create separate frames; the runtimeKey permits parked-frame reuse.
Scenarios.EffectiveConcurrency: The observable recount is synchronous and serialized on the webview main thread. The shared derived observable prevents one AST walk per widget. Widget initialization may have multiple visible frames, while the virtualized factory reuses parked frames; no explicit aggregate creation limiter was visible in repository-owned code.
Scenarios.CacheBehavior: The derived value is shared across transports for a given model update, so multiple widgets reuse one count. Any subsequent document invalidation recomputes the complete count even when totals are unchanged. Removed frames are parked and reused by runtimeKey; disposing the editor removes frames/transports. The guest HTML is self-contained and performs no guest requests.
Scenarios.MechanismConfidence: High: tests and code establish synchronous immediate updates, one shared derived count, exhaustive traversal, and per-widget publication.
Scenarios.MagnitudeUncertainty: AST sizes and task-widget counts vary; the browser tests establish multiple simultaneous frames but not production-scale timing.
Scenarios.Verdict: The iframe/message fan-out is intrinsic and bounded by explicit widget count, but the collection-wide recount on every edit is a reportable repeated-work regression for large documents.

Scenarios.Scenario: Change the VS Code theme while live embedded editors are active or parked
Scenarios.CriticalPath: Theme changes mutate root style/theme-kind attributes; a MutationObserver obtains current CSS and the existing iframe factory forwards it to active and parked frames. This is off normal typing/startup paths and only runs on theme mutations.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Forward updated theme CSS across embedded iframe boundaries
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: At most the observer notifications generated by root style and theme-kind mutations, then one factory-managed update per allocated runtime.
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: Initial iframe theme CSS existed, but live theme-change forwarding did not.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: Required for visible embedded editors to reflect a user-initiated theme change; not on ordinary input or initial rendering beyond initial CSS generation.

Scenarios.ScalingInput: Observer callbacks scale with theme attribute mutations; forwarding scales with the number of allocated iframe runtimes, including parked reusable frames.
Scenarios.EffectiveConcurrency: A single MutationObserver watches two attribute targets per editor. Delivery is browser-batched by mutation microtasks; iframe updates are managed by the factory.
Scenarios.CacheBehavior: Current theme CSS is regenerated from document styles on notification. Parked frames are deliberately retained and updated for reuse, then disposed with the factory/editor. There is no network, filesystem, subprocess, or database boundary.
Scenarios.MechanismConfidence: High for observer reachability and lifecycle; moderate for internal per-frame implementation details.
Scenarios.MagnitudeUncertainty: The dependency's exact per-frame update implementation is outside repository sources, but theme changes are infrequent and allocated frame counts are user-controlled.
Scenarios.Verdict: No additional finding: the work is event-bounded, tied to an explicit theme change, and the observer/factory are disposed.

Scenarios.Scenario: Create the extension-host webview initial state for the live Markdown editor
Scenarios.CriticalPath: The extension serializes the existing initial-state object into the webview HTML. Three small localized task-progress label strings are added to that existing serialization.
Scenarios.ScalingInput: Fixed-size metadata once per editor webview; it does not scale with document tasks or AST nodes.
Scenarios.EffectiveConcurrency: One synchronous initial-state construction/encoding per editor creation, with independent editors handled by their own webviews.
Scenarios.CacheBehavior: No cache is used or needed for these fixed labels. Localization lookup is fixed cardinality. No additional network, filesystem, subprocess, database, or IPC call is introduced beyond the pre-existing webview HTML delivery.
Scenarios.MechanismConfidence: High from the changed initial-state construction and encoding call.
Scenarios.MagnitudeUncertainty: None material; the added payload is three bounded strings.
Scenarios.Verdict: No finding: the fixed metadata addition is negligible and does not create scaling or repeated boundary work.

Analysis.Summary: Completed the performance pass over all 16 changed files and all diff pages. Reported three diff-caused regressions: unconditional iframe-subsystem loading for ordinary fences, eager inclusion of the self-contained guest in every editor entry, and synchronous full-AST recounting on every document edit with a widget. Checked frame/transport cleanup, runtime reuse, theme propagation, serialization, cold/warm resource behavior, and boundary fan-out; no subprocess or database paths were introduced, and no concrete regression-fix learning signal was present.

Stats.CostNote: Copilot SDK reports nano-AI units and model billing multipliers; it does not provide a USD conversion.
